examples: This year is hotter than last year.
This smartphone is lighter than the previous model.
I am taller than my younger brother.
He is better at Japanese than I am.
The bus takes longer than the train.
Between A and B, A is more popular.
fields.explain:
より can be replaced by よりも to emphasize the contrast.
With nouns of time/place, は is often omitted:今年は去年より～.
When answering a どちら question, のほうが is natural: AのほうがBより～/Aのほうが～.
Negative comparison: AはBほど～ない (A is not as ～ as B).

Expresses “A is more than B in terms of ～”. より is placed after the reference target to compare the difference.
The clause after より is the point of reference; the predicate applies to A.
Combine with degree adverbs (ずっと,少し, かなり, やや) to quantify the difference.
With verbs: compares the frequency/degree of an action (食べる/使う/勉強する...).
fields.notes:
Chained comparison: AはBよりCより～ can be ambiguous; it is better to split the sentence or use数値 to make it clear.
With numerical data, state it directly:去年より3%増えた。
Comparing yourself over time:前より/以前より/昔より +形容詞/動詞.
mistakes: Swapping A and B by mistake: × BはAより… (the meaning becomes B is more than A) → note “AはBより…”.
Using を after より: × Aよりを… → より does not take を; it is followed by the predicate.
Confusing it with ほど in affirmative sentences: × AはBほど高い → ほど is used with the negative when comparing more/less.
Leaving out のほうが when answering a comparison question makes the sentence unnatural in conversation.

examples:

fields.explain:
Replaces a noun that appeared earlier.

の～：the ~ one

fields.name: Using quantities and counters
fields.meaning: Position of the counter in the sentence: after Nを/が, before V
examples:
A: How many bottles of beer are there on the desk?
B: There are six.

A: How many people are in the meeting room?
B: There are four.
fields.explain: Quantities and counters always come after the particle.

fields.meaning:
Used to talk about how many times you do something.
なんかい：How many times?
examples: I watch movies twice a week.
Nam goes back home to the countryside once a month.

fields.name: Particles used with means of transportation
fields.meaning:
Get on (a vehicle/train) ~
Get off (a vehicle/train) ~
Change (vehicles/trains) from ~ to ~
～を leave, get out of ~

fields.connection: N(means of transportation) + に + 乗ります / N + を + 降ります / N1 + から + N2 + に + 乗り換えます
examples:
I get on the train.
I get off the train.
I change from the train to a bus.

fields.name: N が A of emotion, degree
fields.meaning: N is A (adjectives of emotion/degree: 頭がいい)
examples: I'm bad at kanji.

A: What do you dislike?
B: I dislike cigarettes.
fields.explain: が： used with adjectives that express emotion or degree.

fields.name: N1(person/thing/place) の N2 position
fields.meaning:
On/above　した：Under/below
In front　うしろ：Behind
Right　ひだり：　Left
Inside　そと：Outside
Next to
Next to ( side by side)
Near
Between
examples: My house is near the park.
Mr. Miller is in the meeting room.

fields.meaning: The particle に indicates the place N1 where N2 ends up after the action V is performed.
fields.connection: N1 (place) + に + N2 + を + V
examples: Please park your car here.
Please write your address here.
Hokkaido gets a lot of snow.

A: What is Maria like?
B: Maria has big eyes and fair skin.

A: Which one is Yumiko?
B: The person with long black hair.
In the room, there are things like a TV and a refrigerator.
At the supermarket, I bought things like meat and eggs.
fields.explain:
Used to list nouns.
For the last N, we do not use や but use など to end the list. など comes before the appropriate particles, depending on the verb at the end of the sentence.
や + など gives a sense of “just examples”, suitable when you do not need to (or cannot) list everything.
In conversation, you can use just や without adding など if the list is implicitly clear.
など comes after the last item in the list, or after a single item, to mean “for example”.
When talking about people: avoid Nなど if you do not want to sound impolite; “先生など” can sound belittling.
fields.notes:
original notes: “NやNなどのN” is often used in headings/reports: “AやBなどの影響”.
“などと +言う/思う” carries a quoting nuance with a dismissive tone:彼が天才だなどと言う。 (implies skepticism).
When the list is long, you can use “などを中心に/などについて”.
meaning_vi: A conjunctive particle that connects a noun with another noun. Used to list a few things out of many.
examples: 1. ①　秋葉原や　原宿。
Akihabara and Harajuku.

fields.name: Joining simple sentences into a compound sentence
fields.meaning: Joining compound sentences: Vて/Aくて/Naで/Nで join clauses with the same topic
examples: Every day I get up at 6, eat breakfast, and then go to school.
I am an office worker, and Mr. Tanaka is a doctor.
I'm Hung, and I'm a student.
This piece of wood is long and heavy.
This place is beautiful and quiet.
fields.explain:
Used to form a compound sentence.
With V: use Vて to list actions in sequence.With N: it can be used not only for sentences with the same topic but also to join sentences with different topics.With A: only used to join adjectives that are similar in meaning.

fields.name: Joining several kinds of things with different quantities
fields.meaning: Listing several kinds of things with different quantities (N1を…とN2を…)
fields.connection: ～は + N1を/が + [quantity] + と + N2を/が + [quantity] + V
examples: On the desk there are two eggs, one piece of bread, and a cup of coffee.

A: Two apples and three bananas, please.
B: Certainly.
fields.explain: The particle depends on the verb at the end of the sentence.

examples: It's raining.
Mr. Miller isn't here, is he?

fields.meaning: The particle に indicates the place where the subject ends up after performing the action V.
examples: You must not go in here.
May I sit on this chair?
fields.explain:
Verbs used:
Nに～
はいります enter N
すわります sit on N
のります get on N (vehicle/train)
のぼります climb N (mountain)
つきます arrive at N
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Move to N (NにV of movement: 日本に行く)
explain: The particle に indicates the destination and is used in place of the direction particle へ.
Verbs such as いきます/きます/かえります/しゅっちょうします can be used with both Nへ and Nに.
examples: 1. A: どこかで　財布を　落として　しまったんです。
B: それは　大変ですね。すぐ　交番に　行かないと。
I've gone and dropped my wallet somewhere.
That's terrible. You need to go to the police box right away.

fields.name: Nは～にいます/あります N is at ～
fields.meaning: N is located at… (います for people and living things, あります for objects)
fields.connection: N + は + N (place) + に + います / あります
examples:
A: Where is the Japanese book?
B: It's on the desk.

A: Where is the cat?
B: It's in the box.
fields.explain: Used to emphasize the location of an object that both the speaker and the listener know about.

fields.name: Equal comparison
examples: A is about as tall as B.
A is the same age as B.
fields.explain: N 1 and N 2 are the same (in some property or characteristic)

fields.name: Less-than comparison
examples: Bananas are not as expensive as apples.

A: What is A's room like?
B: A's room is not as spacious as B's room.
fields.explain: ほど used with a negative ending means that N 1 does not have the property A as much as N 2 .

fields.name: Turning the object into the topic
fields.meaning: When we want to take the direct object in a “NをV” sentence and make it the topic, we replace the particle を with は and move Nは to the beginning of the sentence.
fields.connection: N + を + V → N + は + V (moving the object up to become the topic)
examples:
Please don't put your luggage here.
As for your luggage, please don't put it here.

I eat lunch at the company cafeteria.
As for lunch, I eat it at the company cafeteria.
I want to go to Japan.
What do you want to eat?
I don't want to go home early today.
When I was a child, I wanted to have a dog.
He seems to want to buy a new smartphone.
I want to drink some water.
fields.explain:
Basic politeness in everyday communication; with superiors/customers, use ～たいと思っております／～させていただきたいです to sound softer.
Asking about the listener's wishes: ～たいですか／何が～たいですか; more formal: ～たいでしょうか／～たいですかね.
To emphasize a lasting desire: ～たいと思っています (an intention that has already formed); light and spontaneous: ～たいです.
In complex sentences: can be used before から・ので・けど to give a reason/suggestion:早く帰りたい ので、先に失礼します。

Expresses the speaker's subjective desire or intention “want to do V”; polite with です.
Restriction on the subject: usually used for the first person; asking the second person is fine; for the third person, use ～たがる／～たがっています to make it objective.
Grammatical nature: ～たい is an i-adjective and conjugates like an い-adj (たくない・たかった...).
Particles: the object often changes from を → が when emphasizing the desire toward the target.
Nuance: direct and natural; more formal: ～たいと思っています／～たいと考えています.
fields.notes:
It is unnatural to state a strong desire directly to a superior: “休みたいです” → consider “体調が優れないので、お休みをいただきたいです”。
Avoid “～たいですと思います” (redundant); “～たいと思います” is enough.
Verbal nouns with する: Nを/が＋したい (勉強をしたい／勉強がしたい) are both correct; が emphasizes the desire.
When asking about general preferences:何がしたい？ (casual) instead of何をしたい？ sounds natural.
mistakes: Using it directly for the third person: ×彼は帰りたいです → ◯彼は帰りたがっています.
Mixing up particles: ×水を飲みたい (not wrong), but it is more natural when asking/answering about preferences:水が飲みたい.
Conjugating it like a noun/na-adjective: ×行きたいですな → ◯行きたいです.
Mixing it up with欲しい: ×食べ物がたい → ◯食べ物がほしい／寿司を食べたい.
JLPT: often tests conjugating たい like an い-adj and distinguishing ～たい vs ～たがる.

examples: I have a test tomorrow, so I have to study tonight.
I'm sick, so I have to take medicine.

fields.connection: あまり + [negative predicate] (Vません / Aくない / Naではない / Nがない)
examples: I don't have much time.
This movie isn't very interesting.
I don't eat meat very much.
Japanese isn't very difficult.
There aren't many people here.
I didn't study much yesterday.
fields.explain:
Used to soften the degree of negation and to be polite in communication.
With na-adjectives: ではありません (polite), じゃない (casual).
With nouns of quantity: Nが/は あまり ありません to say “there isn't much/aren't many …”.
Not used for absolute emphasis. To emphasize “almost not”, use ほとんど～ない.

Expresses a degree/duration/frequency LOWER than expected: “not very …/not much …”.
Must be used with the negative form: ありません／ない. Using the affirmative is incorrect in this meaning.
Scope: applies to verbs (actions, frequency), adjectives (degree), and nouns of quantity/existence.
The nuance is gentle and neutral; it is not an absolute negation (unlike全然～ない: “not at all”).
Colloquial variant: あんまり (casual). Polite: ～ません／～ではありません.
fields.notes:
In spoken language, あまり may be slightly clipped before ない: “あまり食べない → まり食べない” (not recommended in exams).
With i-adjectives, both くない and くありません are correct; choose according to the level of politeness.
With quantity words/counters:数はあまり多くない(the number is not large) → more natural when you add evaluative words多く/少なく.
mistakes: Using the affirmative after あまり: × あまり食べます → it must be ○ あまり食べません.
Forgetting to change the i-adjective ending: × あまり高いない → ○ あまり高くない.
Confusing it with全然/ほとんど in degree of negation; choosing wrongly gives the wrong nuance.
Wrong particle for existence: ×人はあまりありません → people are living beings → いません.

rows: あまり～ない／ありません
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>はあまり<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くない。

この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>はそんなに<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しくない。

examples: How many apples are there?
How many pieces of cake did you eat?
How many mandarin oranges did you buy?
Excuse me, but may I ask how old you are?
How many boxes are there here?
I have a few questions.
fields.explain:
Friendly and neutral; when politeness or sensitivity is needed (asking someone's age), use おいくつですか and add the softener失礼ですが.
If the exact unit is needed, use何＋counter: ビンは何本ですか。
In written language, いくつか has a gentle nuance of “a few”, without specifying an exact number.

いくつ asks about an unspecified quantity and is usually used for small items that can be counted directly.
It can replace何＋counter in basic communication; however, with specific units (本、枚、冊…),何＋counter is more natural.
おいくつですか is used politely to ask someone's age (especially older people).
いくつか (noun) means “a few, some”.
fields.notes:
When the quantity is large/not directly countable, switch to どのくらい/どれくらい: どのくらい買いましたか。
Avoid asking someone's age directly when it is not necessary; if you must ask, use おいくつですか to be polite.
In answers, use数字＋counter or a plain number: 3つ／三つ (both kanji and native Japanese forms are fine at N5).
mistakes: Confusing it with いくら (price): × これはいくつですか → ○ これはいくらですか。
Forgetting to use a counter when needed: × ペンはいくつですか (ambiguous) → ○ ペンは何本ですか。
Using いくつ to ask an older person's age without politeness; use おいくつですか／何歳ですか instead.

rows: <ruby>卵<rt>たまご</rt></ruby>はいくつありますか。
Specific about the type of unit
<ruby>卵<rt>たまご</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby><ruby>個<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ですか。
あなたは<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby><ruby>歳<rt>さい</rt></ruby>ですか。
<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>ですが、おいくつですか。

examples: I want to go to Japan someday.
Someday I will have my own shop.
Eventually, I want to buy a house.
I found a photo from some time ago.
I will keep that promise someday.
Let's meet up someday.
fields.explain:
Creates a vague but positive feeling; often used with きっと／必ず to strengthen the commitment.
Use いつかの when talking about an unspecified day in the past that is implicitly shared between the speaker and the listener.
When stating long-term goals, いつかは is placed before the topic to emphasize “sooner or later …”.

Indicates an unspecified point in time in the future (usually) or in the past (when using いつかの). Translation: “someday”.
Carries a nuance of hope/dreams/long-term direction when used with ～たい, ～つもり, ～ます.
いつかは means “eventually …”, emphasizing inevitability without making clear when.
Not used to ask “when”; that is いつ (interrogative).
fields.notes:
To make a goal more concrete, add a vague time reference:将来/いつの日か日本で働きたい。
Avoid overusing it in schedules that require a time commitment; いつか is so vague that it may be taken as evasive.
In spoken language, いつかさ… can introduce an old story/a memory (casual).
mistakes: Confusing it with the interrogative いつ (when): × いつか来ますか (vague) when a specific appointment is needed → ○ いつ来ますか。
Using いつか in a context that requires a clear promise of time (listening section) → trap: the “unspecified” answer choice is more correct.
Confusing いつも/いつでも with いつか because they all contain いつ: pay attention to frequency vs a vague point in time.

rows: いつか<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>したい。
Indicates frequency, not a vague point in time
いつも<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいです。
いつでも<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>してください。

examples: If anything comes up, please contact me anytime.
I can go anytime.
This shop is always open.
If you're ever in trouble, I'll help you anytime.
You can ask questions anytime.
fields.explain:
Used to show flexibility:予約は いつでも 変更できます (You can change your reservation at any time).
Polite/encouraging: いつでもどうぞ／いつでもお越しください sounds friendly and warm.
In advertising/services: サポートは いつでも OK (24/7 support).
Rarely used directly with the negative; when negated, it is more natural to shift the meaning: いつでもは行けません (I can't go just any time) rather than a total negation.

Main meaning: “anytime”, expressing ability/willingness/permission at any point in time.
Polite nuance: often used when making a suggestion or an invitation, or when talking about flexibility of time.
Different from “いつも”: いつでも = “any time is fine (your choice)”; いつも = “always (habit/frequency)”.
Often used with verbs of ability/availability:行ける,会える,使える,開いている,連絡する,手伝う.
Often used in invitations/services: いつでもどうぞ／いつでもお越しください。
fields.notes:
Combining with “Xでも” forms a universal series: いつでも・どこでも・だれでも・なんでも.
In spoken language, “いつでもOK” is colloquial; more formal: “いつでも結構です／差し支えありません”.
Often used with a light condition:困ったら、いつでも～ /必要なら、いつでも～.
mistakes: Confusing it with いつも: いつでもは行きます (wrong meaning) → いつも行きます (I always go).
Unnatural total negation: × いつでも行けません → いつでもは行けません (I can't go just any time).
Position: place it right before the verb/predicate; avoid inserting it in the middle of a long noun phrase, which causes ambiguity.
For the advertising sense of “24/7”, use いつでも; for habits/frequency, you must use いつも.

rows: いつも <ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きする
いつか <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい
いつでもいい／<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>
<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>は いつでもいいです

examples: I always get up at 7.
He is always full of energy.
I don't usually go by bus, but today I will.
She never drinks coffee.
This shop is always lively.
fields.explain:
Very high frequency: almost every time. If you just mean “often”, consider よく／たいてい.
“いつもは” + a present difference: sets up a frame of contrast.
When complaining, いつも can carry a critical nuance:彼は いつも 遅れる (he is always late).

Meaning: “always/regularly”, indicating high frequency (almost every time).
“いつもは” is used to state a general habit and then contrast it with the present situation.
Can be used with both the affirmative and the negative: いつも行く／いつも行かない.
Casual/standard nuance, suitable for both written and spoken language.
fields.notes:
Polite combination: いつもありがとうございます (Thank you for your continued support).
Emphasizing a difference:今日はいつもより寒い (It's colder today than usual).
In letters/business:平素（へいそ）より＝ふだんより (close in meaning to “いつも”).
mistakes: Confusing it with いつでも (availability) → Choose correctly according to the meaning: frequency vs a time of your choice.
Position: place いつも before the predicate; avoid inserting it between the subject and an important particle, which causes ambiguity.
Critical nuance: using いつも + something negative can sound like criticism.

rows: Neutral, a little weaker than いつも
たいてい <ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる
ふだんは <ruby>早寝<rt>はやね</rt></ruby>です
